title: Reading Sources Together
short: Find where sources agree, where they disagree, and where they answer different questions.
trouble: Learners summarize sources one at a time instead of putting them in conversation.

blocks.html: In Composition you judged whether a source is credible; in rhetorical analysis you read one text closely. A synthesis puts several sources in conversation. Before you can use them, read them together and ask how they relate.

head: Relationship
Means
Signal it with
rows: they reach opposite conclusions on the same question
one accepts the other’s point, with a limit
they don’t conflict; each covers a different part of the issue
A shows the benefit; C shows the cost.

blocks.html: A practice set on school start times (The four sources here are made up for practice; they are not real studies or letters.)

items: Source A, a sleep researcher: teenagers’ body clocks shift later in adolescence, so early starts cut sleep.
Source B, a district transportation memo: a later high school start would require more buses or later elementary routes.
Source C, a student survey: most students who answered want a later start, but many with after-school jobs worry about working later.
Source D, a coach’s letter: later starts push practices toward dark in late fall.

blocks.html: Read sources against each other. For each pair, ask: do they agree, disagree, qualify, or answer different questions? A grid of sources and questions makes the conversation visible.

Summarizing sources one at a time leaves the hard thinking to your reader. Seeing that A and B answer different questions (benefit and cost) is what lets you argue that a later start is worth its cost, or not. The relationships are where your own argument comes from.

blocks.title: Pairs in the set
blocks.q: How do A and B relate? A and C? C and D?
steps: A and B: different questions. A is about students’ sleep; B is about bus costs. They don’t contradict each other.
A and C: mostly agree, since students want what the research suggests; C also qualifies it with a worry about jobs.
C and D: agree on a concern: later afternoons cost something, for jobs and for practices.
blocks.a: A/B different questions; A/C agree, with C qualifying; C/D agree on a cost.

blocks.html: Summarizing sources one at a time instead of putting them in conversation. A paragraph per source (“Source A says … Source B says …”) is a book report. Check: do your sentences name two sources at once and say how they relate?

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: A: Students sleep more with later starts. / E: A study at another school found students slept about the same amount after a later start.
A: Later starts add sleep. / B: Later starts need more buses.
C: Most students want a later start. / A: Teens’ body clocks shift later.
B: More buses would cost money. / D: Practices would run toward dark.
cards.why: Both are costs, but about different things: they don’t conflict.

blocks.cap: How does each pair relate? (Practice sources.)
